CV-02.c01: A combination adds parts that send air back to the trailer and control the **trailer brakes**, on top of the tractor's own air brakes.
**psi** = pounds per square inch, the unit on your air pressure gauge.
A **relay valve** on the trailer sends air from the trailer's own tank to its brakes.
**Spring brakes** are held on by strong springs and released by air; on a trailer they work as the parking brakes.
CV-02.c02: The **trailer hand valve** (trolley valve or Johnson bar) puts on the trailer brakes only; use it **only to test** the trailer brakes.
**Never use it while driving**, because braking only the trailer can make it skid; the foot brake works every brake at once.
**Never use it to park**, because air can leak out and the brakes let go; park with the parking brakes, plus chocks if no spring brakes.
To test, set the trailer brakes with the hand valve, then **tug gently** against them in a **low gear** to confirm they hold.
CV-02.c03: The **tractor protection valve** protects the tractor's own air supply if the trailer breaks away or gets a bad leak.
You control it from the cab with the **trailer air supply** control.
It **closes by itself** when air pressure drops to **20–45 psi**; one website says 25–40, but use 20–45 on the test.
When it closes, no air leaves the tractor and the trailer emergency line is emptied, so the **trailer emergency brakes** come on.
CV-02.c04: On newer vehicles the trailer air supply control is a **red, 8-sided knob**; don't confuse it with the yellow diamond parking brake knob.
**Push in** → air goes to the trailer; **pull out** → trailer air shuts off and the trailer emergency brakes come on.
The knob **pops out by itself** when pressure drops into the **20–45 psi** range, as the tractor protection valve closes.
Older vehicles may use a **lever** that may not work automatically, with "normal" and "emergency" positions.
CV-02.c05: Every combination has **2** air lines linking each unit to the next: the service line and the emergency line.
**Service line** (control or signal line) is **blue**; its pressure, set by foot brake or hand valve, goes to the relay valves.
**Emergency line** (supply line) is **red**; it fills the trailer air tanks and controls the trailer emergency brakes.
Emergency line loses air → trailer emergency brakes **come on** and the tractor protection valve **closes**.
A major service line leak may go unnoticed **until you brake**; then tank pressure drops fast and may set the trailer emergency brakes.
CV-02.c06: **Glad hands** join the tractor's service and emergency lines to the trailer's; clean the couplers and check the **rubber seals** for cracks.
To connect, hold the couplers at 90 degrees, push the seals together, and turn to lock; match **blue = service**, **red = emergency**.
**Crossed lines** on a trailer with spring brakes → spring brakes stay on; on an older trailer without them, you could drive away with **no trailer brakes**.
**Dummy couplers** keep **water and dirt** out of unused lines.
CV-02.c07: Each trailer and each converter dolly carries **at least one** air tank.
The tanks are filled through the **emergency (supply) line**, not the service line.
**Relay valves** send tank air to the brakes; service line pressure tells them **how much**.
**Drain every tank every day**, even with automatic drains, because water and oil buildup can stop the brakes working correctly.
CV-02.c08: **Shut-off valves** are in the service and supply lines at the back of trailers that tow other trailers.
They close off the air lines when no trailer is towed behind.
Rule → all open, except at the **rear of the very last trailer**, which must be **closed** so air doesn't escape.
CV-02.c09: Newer trailers have **spring brakes**; they are not required on converter dollies and trailers built **before 1975**.
Trailers without spring brakes have air-powered **emergency brakes** but **no parking brake**.
Their emergency brakes come on if the emergency line loses pressure, you pull the air supply knob, or the trailer is unhooked.
Those brakes hold only while tank air lasts, so **always chock the wheels** when parking a trailer without spring brakes.
CV-02.c10: Every trailer and converter dolly built on or after **March 1, 1998** must have ABS.
Trailers have a **yellow** ABS malfunction lamp on the **left side**, front or rear corner; on older units, look underneath for the ECU and wheel speed sensor wires.
ABS doesn't add braking power or necessarily shorten stops; it works only when a wheel is about to lock, helping you **keep control**.
**Brake as you always have**, whether ABS is on the tractor, trailer, or both; with trailer-only ABS, ease off if a tractor jackknife begins.
If ABS fails you still have **regular brakes**; get it serviced soon, and never drive faster or closer because of ABS.
